clinician.trajectory_summary: A 46-year-old woman sustained a left femoral comminuted fracture with dislocation from a motor vehicle accident. She was alert on arrival but developed sleepiness approximately 5 hours post-injury. By day 2 post-fracture, she presented to the neurology department with severe neurological deterioration (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4), positive bilateral Babinski signs, positive Kernig sign, and neck stiffness. Vital signs on day 2 showed hypertension (148/80 mm Hg), tachycardia (124 bpm), and hypoxemia (PO2 64 mm Hg). Imaging on day 2 revealed bilateral lung exudative lesions with pleural effusion on CT, and diffuse abnormal signals in bilateral cerebral hemispheres, brainstem, and cerebellum on MRI consistent with embolization. By day 14, lung symptoms and CT findings showed considerable improvement. On day 15, transthoracic echocardiography identified shunts through a patent foramen ovale (PFO), which likely facilitated paradoxical embolism of fat globules to the cerebral circulation. The patient was managed with active supportive care and hormone therapy, and was discharged with dysphasia as a residual neurological deficit.
